content: 1. The conditions influencing food systems include economic incentives, subsidies, regulations, trade policies, procurement strategies, market access, and technological advancements. These factors collectively shape the nutritional and health status of individuals, households, and populations. 2. Dietary quality and food security are directly impacted by drivers such as land use changes, over-harvesting, climate change, pollution, and the introduction of invasive species. These factors also affect biodiversity within food systems at genetic, species, and ecosystem levels, including terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems. 3. Indirect drivers, such as demographic and socio-cultural factors, as well as economic and technological developments, play a significant role in shaping food systems. These drivers influence socio-cultural fulfillment, community cohesion, and a sense of place, all of which are integral to health and well-being. 4. The loss of genetic biodiversity in crops reduces the potential to mitigate losses in productivity caused by insect pests and vector-borne crop viruses. Polycultures, which typically have lower pest incidences, are underutilized in modern agricultural practices. 5. Increasing crop biodiversity in managed agroecosystems can effectively reduce the reliance on pesticides while enhancing ecological and climate resilience. For instance, plant biodiversity contributes to the regulation and provision of water, soil, and air quality. 6. Buffer strips of permanent vegetation along water bodies not only provide critical wildlife habitats but also reduce the runoff of nutrients, chemicals, sediments, and pesticides from agricultural lands. This practice improves water quality and reduces soil erosion. 7. Agro-biodiversity maximizes agronomic, environmental, and economic benefits while mitigating the negative impacts of chemical inputs and pollution associated with modern agriculture. It also supports farmers in increasing yields and optimizing health outcomes through mixed farming systems and holistic strategies that promote long-term soil fertility. 8. The global shift away from traditional agricultural models has placed significant pressure on agro-biodiversity. Industrial agriculture, deforestation, land conversion, freshwater depletion, and the intensification of production systems have led to the erosion of genetic diversity and the proliferation of monocultures. 9. Conventional high-input agriculture relies on landscape simplification and mechanized production processes, resulting in declines in genetic and species diversity. This undermines key agroecosystem functions and exacerbates the effects of climate change, pollution, and other global environmental changes. 10. The global food and trade marketplace drives industrial agriculture, creating a complex web of land-use changes, fertilizer and pesticide use, commercial seed sales, and agricultural policies that favor agribusiness. This system influences the types of crops grown and their distribution, ultimately affecting the nutritional quality of diets. 11. The increasing consumption of meat, particularly in affluent and developed countries, places additional pressure on agroecosystems. Producing 1 kg of meat requires 3–10 kg of grain, and livestock grazing occupies about one-quarter of the Earth's land area, accounting for 70% of agricultural land use. 12. Livestock production contributes significantly to greenhouse gas emissions through enteric fermentation, manure, feed production, and downstream processes like transportation and storage. It also requires substantial water resources, with over 90% of water use linked to animal feed production. 13. Livestock systems have low production efficiency, leaking nutrients into water and air and generating large volumes of manure and by-products. Only about 20% of the nitrogen and phosphorus in feed crops are converted into food, with the rest contributing to environmental pollution. 14. Soil biodiversity is critical for food security, nutrition, and health. It filters water and pollutants, enhances crop yield and nutrient content, reduces pests and diseases, and protects against foodborne, waterborne, and soilborne illnesses. 15. Soil erosion and degradation pose significant challenges to food security and health. Agroecological practices like soil mulching and cover crop cultivation improve soil quality, crop health, and resilience to pests, reducing food loss and waste. 16. Microbial diversity in soil and the environment plays a vital role in regulating the immune system through interactions with gut microbiota. The human microbiome, a complex ecological network, supports digestion, nutrient absorption, and protection against pathogens. 17. Diets that promote microbial diversity in the gut are linked to better gut health, while others contribute to non-communicable diseases (NCDs) like obesity and diabetes. Reduced exposure to environmental microorganisms has been associated with increased rates of inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. 18. Biodiversity loss at the microbial level may affect gut health and NCDs through environmental and dietary pathways. This highlights the importance of preserving biodiversity to maintain health and nutrition. 19. The loss of biodiversity in food systems, coupled with increased reliance on processed and ultra-processed foods, simplifies human diets and reduces their nutritional value. The decline in genetic diversity of crops and breeds further limits food choices and nutritional quality. 20. From an estimated 50,000 edible plant species, only three crops (wheat, rice, and maize) provide over 50% of plant-derived calories globally. This reliance on a few crops reduces dietary diversity and resilience. 21. Wild foods, including fish, plants, and fungi, are essential for dietary diversity and nutrition, particularly as sources of micronutrients. However, their consumption can sometimes pose health risks, especially when improperly handled or cooked. 22. Unsafe food causes an estimated 600 million cases of foodborne diseases and 420,000 deaths annually, with children under five years old accounting for 30% of these deaths. Foodborne illnesses are often infectious or toxic in nature and can result from pathogens or chemical contaminants. 23. The use of antimicrobials in food production has led to the emergence of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria, posing significant public health risks. Food safety is a critical component of health security, requiring cross-sectoral capacity to prevent, detect, and manage foodborne disease risks.
